name: rpg-cli
why: Turns your filesystem into a role-playing dungeon, a playful idea that makes you see directories differently.

brief.what_it_is: rpg-cli is a minimalist computer role-playing game written in Rust, played from the command line. Its CLI works as a cd replacement: as you change directories, the hero walks deeper into the filesystem, and enemies sometimes appear and battle automatically. Input is ordinary shell commands like cd, ls, buy and todo, and the output is a text status block showing HP, MP, XP, stats, equipment and gold. The hero's location is the working directory, and directories farther from home hold tougher enemies and treasure chests.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted to strip a JRPG down to its underlying mechanics, "the simplest thing that could possibly pass as a video game," and the command line was the narrowest interface he could think of. The blog post describes it as a constraint that fostered creativity and as a side project meant to yield something usable within a few months.
brief.how_it_works: The game keeps its own record of the hero's location and turns directory changes into movement, rolling for random encounters on the way. Battles are fully automatic: each side acts according to its speed stat, and the player's default action is to attack unless HP is low and a potion is available. Because a program cannot change its parent shell's directory, a small shell function forwards arguments to rpg-cli and then runs cd to the path rpg-cli pwd reports. Death is permanent, and a tombstone left in the dead hero's directory can be looted by a new hero.

commands_seen.context: Installs rpg-cli from source at tag 1.2.0 via Cargo, the Rust package manager; the binary lands in ~/.cargo/bin.
Homebrew install on macOS, as listed in the README's other-methods section.
Basic shell wrapper function that runs rpg-cli and then moves the shell to the hero's location. Written in the README as a multi-line sh function.

commands_seen.cmd: cd () { rpg-cli cd "$@"; builtin cd "$(rpg-cli pwd)"; }
commands_seen.context: The hardcore version from the README: overrides the built-in cd so that every directory change moves the hero and can trigger battles.
Re-rolls the hero with new random stats; the README shows it before running rpg to view the new character.
Switches the hero to the mage class, which enables magic attacks and an MP bar.
Moves the hero into the dev/ subdirectory, which can trigger random battles along the way.
Inspects the current directory for hidden treasure chests.
Lists items sold in the home directory, with prices in gold, such as sword, shield, potion, remedy and escape.
Shows the hero's quest checklist, which renews as the level rises and gives rewards for completed items.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows are on the GitHub releases page. Building with Cargo needs a Rust toolchain. Other channels are Homebrew (macOS), Nixpkgs, Portage (Gentoo) and pacman (Arch extra repo). The binary must be on PATH, and for a cargo install that means ~/.cargo/bin. No accounts or runtimes beyond that are needed. For real cd integration, add the shell function to your rc file; the README gives fish equivalents in its shell integration guide. Custom character classes can go in ~/.local/share/rpg/classes.yaml, and the README points to the dirs crate docs for the data path on other OSes.
brief.standout: Auto-battle is borrowed from Suikoden 2's auto-battle button, and the classic JRPG stats are cut down to hp, strength and speed. Equipment is generic and level-based (sword[1], sword[5]), so stronger gear replaces weaker gear without any selling. Using cd as the way to explore a dungeon, with difficulty set by distance from home, is an unusual framing that is hard to find elsewhere.
brief.status: Unknown from the sources I read. The homepage is a blog post dated 2024-07-16 that calls rpg-cli a fondest personal project and describes its history back to 2021. The README pins the install tag to 1.2.0 and lists packages in Homebrew, Nixpkgs, Gentoo and Arch extra, which suggests it is active enough to be packaged. I saw no last-commit or last-release date, so I cannot confirm whether development is ongoing.
brief.caveats: The macOS release binary is not signed, so the first launch needs right-click, then Open. Death is permanent and the game is hard to play well: the README says going too far or too long without healing will likely get your hero killed. Gameplay is non-interactive, so there are no choices during battle beyond the auto-battle rules. The cd override is invasive and can confuse other shell habits. The blog post says the author dropped a follow-up roguelike, rpg-tui, and the README does not mention that project. The license was not in the README text I read.
quotes: rpg-cli is a minimalist computer RPG written in Rust. Its command-line interface can be used as a cd replacement where you randomly encounter enemies as you change directories.
Death is permanent: you can't save your progress and reload after dying, but if you take your new hero to the location of the previous one's death, you can recover gold, items and equipment.
To me, a classic JRPG is pure mechanism, a kind of puzzle.

entry.title: rpg-cli
entry.tldr: A tiny JRPG where cd is the movement command: the deeper you wander from home, the tougher the monsters, and your filesystem becomes the dungeon.
entry.deeper_look:
rpg-cli is a minimalist role-playing game written in Rust. You play it with ordinary shell commands. `cd` moves the hero, `ls` looks for treasure chests, `buy` lists the shop, and `todo` shows a quest checklist. Output is a plain text status block with HP, MP, XP, stats, equipment and gold. Distance from your home directory sets the difficulty, so farther directories hold tougher enemies and better loot.

The author, Facundo Olano, wanted to strip a JRPG down to its mechanics, "the simplest thing that could possibly pass as a video game." The command line was the narrowest interface he could think of. In his words, "a classic JRPG is pure mechanism, a kind of puzzle." Battles are fully automatic, borrowing the auto-battle button from Suikoden 2. Each side acts by its speed stat, and the hero attacks unless HP is low and a potion is on hand. Stats are cut down to HP, strength and speed, and gear is generic and level-based (sword[1], sword[5]), so better equipment simply replaces worse.

There is a neat Unix lesson underneath. A program cannot change its parent shell's directory, so the game keeps its own record of where the hero is. A small shell function calls rpg-cli, then runs `cd` to whatever `rpg-cli pwd` reports. The README also offers a hardcore variant that overrides the built-in `cd`, so every directory change can start a fight.

Death is permanent. There is no save and reload, but a tombstone stays in the directory where the hero died. A new hero who walks there can recover the gold, items and equipment.
entry.install:
brew install rpg-cli
# Then add a wrapper function to your shell rc file so the shell follows the hero:
rpg () { rpg-cli "$@"; cd "$(rpg-cli pwd)"; }
# Prebuilt binaries and `cargo install` (needs a Rust toolchain) are also options. Fish users: see the shell integration guide.

try_this.what_happens: Re-rolls the hero with new random stats, then you can run `rpg` to see the new character.
Moves the hero into a subdirectory, possibly triggering random battles along the way.
Lists what the home directory shop sells, with gold prices: sword, shield, potion, remedy and escape.

entry.whats_unique: Using `cd` as the way to explore a dungeon, with difficulty set by distance from home, is an unusual framing that is hard to find elsewhere. Auto-battle and three stats keep it very small.
entry.caveats: Death is permanent and the game is hard to play well; the README warns that going too far without healing will likely kill your hero. The cd override can confuse other shell habits, and the unsigned macOS release binary needs right-click, then Open.
